Title: AI hardware demand increases tin’s exposure to supply disruption - Fastmarkets
URL: https://www.fastmarkets.com/insights/ai-hardware-demand-increases-tins-exposure-to-supply-disruption/
Published: 2026-08-25T08:16:31.000Z
Author: Rory Deng
Highlights:
## The AI hardware chain is becoming a material source of tin procurement exposure, particularly within solder, but its market impact cannot be assessed by adding a single headline number to the global supply-demand balance. Our bottom-up model covers 26 component lines across data center equipment, client and edge devices, AI-enabled vehicles, industrial automation, drones and humanoid robots.
...
Gross AI-chain procurement exposure rises from 11.34 thousand tonnes in 2026 to 26.51 thousand tonnes in 2030. The product-counterfactual increment – the tin consumed by AI equipment after deducting the conventional equipment assumed to be displaced – increases from 6.40 thousand tonnes to 17.05 thousand tonnes.
...
The solder-related subset rises from 10.16 thousand tonnes to 23.64 thousand tonnes, equivalent to 4.8% of global solder tin demand in 2026 and 10.6% in 2030. Our base view is that AI will raise tin’s structural demand floor and increase the market’s sensitivity to supply interruptions.
...
Gross procurement exposure grows at a compound annual rate of approximately 25% between 2025 and 2030. The product-counterfactual increment grows faster than gross exposure after 2026, rising from 56.4% of exposure in 2026 to 64.3% in 2030
...
Under the model’s substitution assumptions, AI deployment therefore becomes progressively more additive rather than purely replacing conventional equipment.
...
| Model measure | 2025 | 2026 | 2028 | 2030 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All-chain exposure (kt) | 8.66 | 11.34 | 17.94 | 26.51 |
| Product increment (kt) | 4.99 | 6.4 | 10.85 | 17.05 |
| Solder-related subset (kt) | 7.73 | 10.16 | 16.04 | 23.64 |
| Product increment / global demand | 1.24% | 1.56% | 2.58% | 3.98% |
| Solder subset / solder demand | 3.74% | 4.77% | 7.32% | 10.60% |
...
expanding within tin
...
By 2030, the modeled solder-related subset reaches 10.6% of global solder tin demand. Gross AI-chain exposure is equivalent to 6.2% of total refined tin demand in the same year. These shares remain insufficient to create a shortage independently, but they are large enough to affect the marginal balance, particularly when supply is slow to respond.
...

...

...
Combining the AI consumption model with our supply-demand balance provides a clearer measure of its potential market significance. Our balance model forecasts refined-tin deficits of approximately 9 thousand tonnes in 2026 and 8 thousand tonnes in 2027.
...
Gross AI-chain procurement exposure is equivalent to 103% of the forecast deficit in 2026, rising to 159% in 2027. The product-counterfactual increment provides the more relevant measure of marginal AI demand. It rises from 58% of the projected deficit in 2026 to 93% in 2027.
...
| Year | Forecast deficit | Gross AI-chain exposure | Gross exposure / deficit | Product-counterfactual increment | Increment / deficit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2026 | 9.0 kt | 14.28 kt | 158.7% | 8.33 kt | 92.5% |
| 2027 | 8.0 kt | 17.94 kt | 224.3% | 10.85 kt | 135.6% |
...
These ratios are comparisons of scale, not automatic additions to the balance. Some growth in electronics and technology-related consumption may already be embedded in the underlying demand forecast. Gross exposure also includes tin that would have been consumed in conventional products without AI. Reconciliation with the existing balance is therefore required before assigning any additional demand.
...
Even with these qualifications, the comparison shows that AI-related demand is becoming material relative to the market’s annual imbalance. By 2027, the modeled product-counterfactual increment is larger than the entire projected deficit. In an already-deficit market, stronger-than-expected AI procurement could accelerate inventory drawdowns, encourage precautionary restocking and intensify competition for available metal.
...
AI is therefore unlikely to create the tin deficit by itself, but it can materially change how the market responds to an existing deficit. Direct AI-chain demand raises the structural consumption floor, while the wider infrastructure cycle represents an additional but unquantified upside channel. Expectations surrounding AI investment may also add a sentiment premium before the associated physical demand becomes visible.
...
Ultimately, physical conditions determine whether that premium is sustained. Under the current combination of forecast deficits, limited visible buffers and slow supply elasticity, AI is becoming both a material source of marginal demand and an amplifier of tin’s sensitivity to the next supply disruption. However, the modelled demand does not provide a price floor in isolation.

Title: Data demand sends tin surging; deficit looms in 2026 | Coface
URL: https://www.coface.com/news-economy-and-insights/tin-is-riding-high-on-the-metals-market-s-latest-surge
Published: 2026-02-05T00:00:00.000Z
Author: N/A
Highlights:
A key metal in the electronics industry — solder alone accounts for 50% of global demand — tin is benefiting greatly from energy and digital transitions. However, supply growth remains limited, particularly in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Myanmar, which is expected to lead to a supply deficit as early as 2026, the first since 2021.
...
## An emerging supply deficit
...
Overall, refined tin production is expected to grow by 3% in 2026, following 2% growth in 2025. This will be insufficient to offset the expected 3.5% increase in demand in 2026. The market is therefore expected to shift into deficit this year, a situation that is likely to continue in the years to come. Finally, in the longer term, the main challenge will be the expansion of mining capacity, as the depletion of exploited deposits is a major vulnerability for the entire value chain.
...
China accounts for 50% of global refined tin production. Despite anti-involution measures, we estimate that Chinese production will remain robust in 2026 (+5%). Tin remains a strategic asset in China's quest for self-sufficiency in data management infrastructure. Conversely, production in neighboring Indonesia 2 could decline, given regulatory constraints and growing aversion to mining projects. Domestic production is expected to fall by 2% in 2026 (after -1% the previous year).
...
The main vulnerability lies in tin ore supplies, particularly from the Democratic Republic of Congo(DRC) and Myanmar, which together account for 20% of global production and 60% of Chinese tin ore imports. In the DRC, frequent skirmishes between M23 rebel forces and the Congolese regular army are having a negative impact on mining operations in North Kivu and regularly disrupting mining, particularly at the Bisie mine (nearly 6% of global production). In Myanmar, a series of operational uncertainties continues to limit tin extraction to levels below original market forecasts.
...
Over the longer term, industrial demand for tin is expected to keep trending higher. The surge in electronic components demand will accelerate further as data‑based technologies request metals-intensive infrastructures. According to SEMI’s latest report, global silicon wafer shipments are expected to rise by 5.2% YoY in 2026 (after +5.4% in 2025), to 13,500 million square inches (MSI). Innovation will improve efficiency, but not nearly enough to contain the surging demand driven by digitalization.
...
In the longer term, demand for tin is expected to continue to grow, driven by the rise of semiconductors and data storage infrastructure, which are voracious consumers of metals. According to the latest SEMI3 report, global shipments of silicon wafers are expected to increase by 5.2% this year, after +5.4% in 2025, to 13,500 MSI4. Innovation will certainly reduce metal intensity, but not enough to offset the growing demand linked to digitalization.

Title: The need for investment in tin future supply - International Tin Association
URL: https://www.internationaltin.org/the-need-for-investment-in-tin-future-supply/
Published: 2024-12-19T00:00:00.000Z
Author: Freddie Mitchell
Highlights:
ITA Senior Market Analyst Tom Langston presented on the Investment Case for Tin. Langston highlighted that tin is already an essential metal, with 50% of tin used in solder, and other uses in chemicals, tinplate, lead-acid batteries, and a variety of alloys. Tin’s use in solder exposes it to the rapidly growing EV and solar industries, which we forecast will push tin consumption up from 357,000 tonnes in 2023 to 428,000 tonnes in 2030.
...
Amid substantial demand growth, the supply picture is more challenging. As 2024 draws to a close, the year has highlighted risks associated with a highly concentrated supply chain: Indonesia, the largest exporter of refined tin, and Myanmar, the largest exporter of tin concentrates, have both seen significant supply disruptions.
...
The dominance of China and Asia is set to cool, with mine supply forecasted to plateau towards 2040. ITA anticipates major mine supply growth in Australia and Europe, with large-scale tin mining forecasted to return to Europe from 2027. A more diversified mine supply picture by 2040 signals stronger security of supply for Asian smelters.
...
However, ITA anticipates demand to outstrip supply by 2028, reaching a market deficit of 13,000 tonnes by 2030. The existing pipeline of tin projects is too thin, and investment has been insufficient in recent years, far below reaching the estimated $1.07 billion required to bring the required mine capacity online.
...
Miller explained the enormous potential for investment
...
that “the issue is the small size of the critical metals space when you take out copper and lithium”. In particular, the tin market’s small size relative to other metals and the smaller size of tin equities represents a possible challenge.
...
The existing pipeline of tin new supply projects may be thin, but these projects represent strong investment opportunities in an industry with robust long-term supply and demand dynamics.

Title: Tin Supply Deficit Persists as Myanmar and Indonesia Constraints Continue | Rzzro
URL: https://rzzro.com/news-insights/tin-supply-deficit-myanmar-indonesia-jun-26-2026.html
Published: 2026-06-26T00:00:00.000Z
Author: N/A
Highlights:
▶ The global refined tin market is estimated to be in a 8,000-10,000 tonne deficit in 2026, the fifth consecutive year of shortfall. Myanmar’s Wa State exports remain at roughly 60% of pre-2023 levels, and Indonesian tin exports are constrained by permitting and ESG compliance. Combined, these two suppliers account for roughly 45% of global tin mine production.
...
2026 Deficit Est.8,000-10,000t5th year
...
Exports~65,000t/yr-15% vs
...
LME Inventories~3,800t~3 days demand
...
Global Mine Output~310,000t+1.2% YoY
...
The International Tin Association (ITA) estimates the global refined tin market deficit at 8,000-10,000 tonnes in 2026, extending a run of annual deficits that began in 2022. The cumulative deficit over five years is approximately 50,000 tonnes — roughly 15% of annual consumption — which explains why LME inventories remain at critically low levels of just 3,800 tonnes, equivalent to approximately three days of global demand.
...
The supply constraints are concentrated in two countries. Myanmar’s Wa State, which accounted for roughly 10% of global tin mine production before 2023, continues to operate well below capacity. The suspension of mining activities announced by the United Wa State Army in August 2023 officially ended in 2024, but exports have recovered to only about 60% of pre-suspension levels. It is unclear when — or whether — full production will resume.
...
Indonesia, the world’s largest tin exporter, shipped roughly 65,000 tonnes of refined tin in 2025 and is on a similar pace in 2026 — down about 15% from the 2023 peak. The decline reflects tighter permitting under Indonesia’s revised mining regulations and increased scrutiny of ESG compliance by international buyers. Several Indonesian smelters have had their export licenses delayed or suspended.
...
New mine supply is not filling the gap. Global tin mine production grew an estimated 1.2% in the first five months of 2026, with modest increases in Peru and the DRC offsetting declines in Myanmar and Indonesia. There are no major new tin mines expected to reach production before 2028. The supply picture is structurally bullish — demand would need to decline by 3-4% to balance the market, and there is no sign of that happening.
...
The tin deficit is structural and will not be resolved by price alone. Myanmar’s production may never fully recover, and Indonesia’s export capacity is constrained by policy, not economics. Buyers should plan for tin prices in the $48,000-55,000 range as the new normal through 2026-2027. The recent selloff below $50,000 was a macro-driven anomaly, not a reflection of improving supply. For procurement teams that use tin in solder or packaging applications, securing H2 supply now is essential. The risk of a supply shock — an Indonesian export ban, a Myanmar disruption — is real and would send prices sharply higher given the lack of inventory buffer.

---
